response.query: What explicit per-task target dataset sizes and per-subgroup quotas (age, sex, comorbidity) are needed to achieve robust generalization for nodule detection, malignancy, ILD staging, COVID/ARDS phenotyping, and treatment-response tasks?
response.answer: For robust generalization in nodule detection, malignancy, ILD staging, COVID/ARDS phenotyping, and treatment-response tasks, datasets should include diverse subgroups with sufficient size, typically over 100 samples per subgroup. Larger datasets improve model performance, but specific per-subgroup quotas are not universally defined.

In general, all models yielded more consistent explanations with the nodule regions when trained on a larger sample size. In contrast, explanation supervision methods (HAICS, RXD-L and RXD-G) are highly dependent on nodule regions, suggesting that explanation supervision methods are able to learn attributions that are more consistent with human cognition. results.title: Age, comorbidity, life expectancy, and pulmonary nodule follow-up in older veterans
results.content: Age, comorbidity, life expectancy, and pulmonary nodule follow-up in older veterans - PMC. Age, comorbidity, life expectancy, and pulmonary nodule follow-up in older veterans. From 2008–09 to 2013–14, the number of older veterans diagnosed with new pulmonary nodules almost doubled, including among those with severe comorbidity and limited life expectancy. Neither the Fleischner Society guidelines [3, 4] for incidental nodules nor the Lung Computed Tomography (CT) Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) [5] guideline for screen-detected nodules provide detailed information on how to incorporate age, comorbidity, or life expectancy to individualize nodule follow-up. As increasing numbers of older patients and their providers face these clinical challenges, it is important to characterize comorbidity and life expectancy in older adults with pulmonary nodules and how these patient factors impact nodule follow-up. We performed a retrospective cohort study to a) characterize age, comorbidity, and life expectancy among veterans age ≥65 with newly diagnosed incidental, symptom-detected, or screen-detected pulmonary nodules in 2008–09 compared to 2013–14 and b) determine the impact of age, comorbidity, and life expectancy on four-year follow-up among the 2008–09 subgroup. Patient and baseline nodule characteristics associated with receipt of any nodule imaging and/or biopsy during four-year follow-up in veterans age ≥65 with newly diagnosed pulmonary nodule(s) in 2008–09 (n = 243). Given the immediate and potentially substantial harms of intensive pulmonary nodule surveillance and invasive procedures, decreased nodule follow-up among patients with severe comorbidity and limited life expectancy may represent appropriate individualization of nodule evaluation where the risks of nodule follow-up outweigh the chance of benefit. Our study has a number of strengths, including a comparison of patient and nodule characteristics over time and a comprehensive examination of the impact of age, comorbidity, and life expectancy on pulmonary nodule evaluation. Data are not yet available to examine four-year follow-up for the subgroup with newly diagnosed pulmonary nodules in 2013–14 after implementation of lung cancer screening and the Lung-RADS guideline. As the number of older patients diagnosed with pulmonary nodules increases over time, nodule follow-up can be individualized by considering comorbidity and life expectancy for all patients, not just those with smaller nodules. 10.1513/AnnalsATS.201406-283OC [DOI] [PMC free article] [PubMed] [Google Scholar%20pulmonary%20nodules&author=CG%20Slatore&author=SE%20Golden&author=L%20Ganzini&author=RS%20Wiener&author=DH%20Au&volume=12&issue=2&publication_year=2015&pages=184-92&pmid=25521482&doi=10.1513/AnnalsATS.201406-283OC&)].

Most recent research on lung nodule detection that used modified state-of-the-art single-stage object detector, Retina U-Net to generate detection/bounding box and classify malignancy status of lung nodule was done by _Jaeger et al._ Their research proves that U-Net integrated within Retina U-Net was able to perform on par with state-of-the-art two-stage object detector, U-Faster R-CNN and Mask R-CNN for lung malignancy detection and classification with their mAP respectively 49.8%, 50.5%, and 48.3% (Jaeger et al., 1811). Add a new dataset here Lung nodule detection and classification from Thorax CT-scan using RetinaNet with transfer learning Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences 2020·Ivan William Harsono, Suryadiputra Liawatimena, Tjeng Wawan Cenggoro· Edit social preview Lung malignancy is one of the most common causes of death in the world caused by malignant lung nodules which commonly diagnosed radiologically by radiologists. To address the problem, this paper proposed a novel lung nodule detection and classification model using one stage detector called as “I3DR-Net.” The model was formed by combining pre-trained natural images weight of Inflated 3D ConvNet (I3D) backbone with feature pyramid network to multi-scale 3D Thorax Computed tomography scan (CT-scan) dataset. I3DR-Net able to produce remarkable results on lung nodule texture detection task with mAP 49.61% and 22.86%, and area under curve (AUC) 81.84% and 70.36% for public and private dataset.

results.title: Deep learning tool improves accuracy of lung nodule malignancy detection
results.content: Deep learning tool improves accuracy of lung nodule malignancy detection * 1Currently rated 5.0 by 1 person Deep learning tool improves accuracy of lung nodule malignancy detection Radiological Society of North AmericaSep 16 2025 An artificial intelligence (AI) deep learning tool that estimates the malignancy risk of lung nodules achieved high cancer detection rates while significantly reducing false-positive results. AI accounts for factors that we might not even see on the CT scan to further assess a nodule as likely to be malignant." > Noa Antonissen, M.D., lead researcher and Ph.D. candidate at Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, the Netherlands Most current lung cancer screening protocols rely on nodule size, type and growth to estimate malignancy risk. In the retrospective study, the researchers trained their in-house developed deep learning algorithm to estimate the risk for malignancy for lung nodules using data from the National Lung Screening Trial which included 16,077 nodules (1,249 malignant). At 100% sensitivity for cancers diagnosed within 1 year, the deep learning model classified 68.1% of benign cases as low risk compared to 47.4% using the PanCan model, representing a 39.4% relative reduction in false positives. "Reducing false positive results will make lung cancer screening more feasible."
